problem_markdown: Two intersecting circles share $A$. Two points start at $A$ and traverse the respective circles in the same direction, each at constant speed, completing one revolution simultaneously. Prove there is a fixed point equidistant from the moving points at every instant.
solutions_markdown:
Let the centres be $O_1,O_2$, and reflect $A$ across the perpendicular bisector of $O_1O_2$ to obtain $P$. Denote this reflection by $S$. At any instant the two radius vectors have undergone the same rotation $R_\theta$. Since reflection reverses rotation, $SR_\theta=R_{-\theta}S$.

Write $u=A-O_1$, $v=A-O_2$, and let $L$ be the linear part of $S$. Then $P-O_2=Lu$ and $P-O_1=Lv$. Thus the squared distances from $P$ are $|R_\theta u-Lv|^2$ and $|R_\theta v-Lu|^2$. Their norm terms agree. Their dot-product terms agree too, since $LR_\theta$ is a reflection and therefore a symmetric linear map:
$$(R_\theta u)\cdot Lv=u\cdot(LR_\theta)v=(R_\theta v)\cdot Lu.$$
Consequently the two distances are equal for every $\theta$.
